study.title: Genesis 35 Purification, renewal of the covenant and close a generation
study.overview: Genesis 35 shows God calling Jacob back to Bethel to fulfill the vow made years earlier. Before worshiping, Jacob's house must abandon foreign idols, purify itself and change clothing, a sign of repentance and exclusivity to the Lord. At Bethel, God confirms Jacob's name change to Israel and reaffirms the promises of offspring and land. The chapter also gathers memories of death and mourning Deborah, Rachel and Isaac - while presenting the birth of Benjamin, the list of the twelve tribes, and the continuity of the family of promise despite failures, losses and sins within the patriarchal house itself.

outline.title: Called Bethel and purification of the house
outline.explanation: God commands Jacob to go up Bethel and build an altar. Jacob responds leading his family to abandon strange gods, wash himself and change clothes, showing that true worship requires exclusivity. The surrender of idols and God's fear of neighboring cities point out that the journey is sustained by divine protection, not by human force.

outline.title: Adoration in Bethel and confirmation of the alliance
outline.explanation: Upon arriving at Bethel, Jacob builds the altar and calls the place of El-Betel, acknowledging that the God who appeared there is the same that preserved it in the way. The death of Deborah introduces a tone of mourning, but soon God appears again, blesses Jacob, confirms the name Israel and reaffirms the promise of a nation, of kings and of the land given to Abraham and Isaac. Jacob responds with a pillar, libel and olive oil, as a memorial of gratitude.

outline.title: Birth of Benjamin and death of Rachel
outline.explanation: On the way to Ephrath, Rachel enters labor and dies when giving birth. The boy receives two names in tension: Benoni, connected to the pain of his mother, and Benjamin, given by his father. Rachel's grave with a spine shows that the promise continues amidst pain, and that the history of the patriarchal family progresses at real cost.

outline.title: Family Rupture, Jacob's offspring and death of Isaac
outline.explanation: Israel dwells on the land when Reuben lies with Bila, a grave sin that will be relevant to future family history. The text then lists the twelve sons of Jacob, consolidating the structure of the covenant people. Finally, Jacob goes to Hebron, Isaac dies with advanced age, and Esau and Jacob burys him together, ending the previous generation and showing family reconciliation in the last service to his father.

study.context: The given notes place the chapter as the closure of a stage in Isaac's history and the strengthening of the line of the covenant through Jacob and his sons. According to commentators, Jacob had already been sent to Bethel and had postponed the fulfillment of the vote made there. The return to Bethel marks a moment of spiritual renewal of the patriarchal house. The chapter also records funerals and family transitions, indicating the passage from one generation to another.
study.theology: The chapter emphasizes that God's covenant is not supported by human merit, but by divine fidelity. Still, the proper response to the Lord includes repentance, removal of idols and exclusive worship. Bethel works as a place of memory: God revealed himself before, preserved Jacob on the way and now confirms the promise again. Jacob's name change to Israel reaffirms identity and vocation: he who fought with God and has now been blessed represents the people in formation. The text also shows that the promise advances through fragile people: there is idolatry, mourning, sexual sin and death, but God continues to lead history. The tension between pain and hope appears in the birth of Benjamin and in Rachel's death, and also in the death of Isaac, who closes an era without ending God's faithfulness.

scholarViews.insight: The chapter highlights the renewal of the faith of Jacob's house so that the covenant could proceed through its children; the removal of idols and pure worship at Bethel mark this transition.
Jacob obeying the call to Bethel implies purifying his house from idols and resuming the fulfillment of the vow made to the Lord, showing that worship requires moral and spiritual preparation.
The name Benoni reflects the pain of childbirth and Raquel's death, but Jacob changes the name to Benjamin, preserving the continuity of the family despite the loss.

questions: What, in practice, needs to be removed from our home or routine for our worship to be exclusive to the Lord?
How does the renewal of the Bethel covenant help us to remember that God reaffirms his promises even after delays, flaws and mournings?
How does the list of the twelve children and the episodes of sin and death show that God leads his story despite human fragility?
study.practice: Apply this chapter by examining your personal and family devotion: abandon any practice, image, habit or rival trust that takes you to the place of God; establish concrete moments of worship, prayer and gratitude; and treat losses and crises as occasions to remember that the Lord remains faithful to his promises. It is also worth noting that sin within Jacob's family had consequences, so domestic holiness is not optional. At the same time, the chapter invites to record the faithfulness of God, as Jacob did with altar, pillar, oil, and names, so that the memory of grace may sustain the journey.
study.uncertainty: The notes provided do not clarify some details mentioned by the biblical text, such as the precise identity and the place of origin of Deborah beyond what appears in the chapter itself. It is also not possible to confirm, from these notes, all the historical aspects of dates, fine geography or ancient funerary customs. The reading presented follows the Protestant evangelical perspective in a non-denominational way and treats interpretations of the commentators as interpretations, not as absolute conclusions.
